title: How India Usurped Cricket's Throne From England and Australia
excerpt: From IPL billions to global franchise ownership, India's financial and competitive dominance has reshaped the sport—though the latest Test rankings show the on-field race remains tight.
body:
• India has overtaken England and Australia as cricket's dominant power, with the BCCI commanding over 80% of global cricket revenue through the IPL and broadcasting deals
  • The IPL's $18.5 billion ecosystem value and $6 billion-plus media rights deal have made Indian cricket franchises worth more than many European football clubs
  • Australia recently dethroned India as the No. 1 ranked Test team, with only two rating points separating the top three teams—the tightest margin since rankings began in 2003
  • Global private equity firms including Blackstone and KKR are pursuing IPL franchise stakes, signaling cricket's emergence as a premium global asset class

The balance of power in world cricket has undergone a transformation so complete that the sport's traditional custodians—England and Australia—now operate in the shadow of India's financial and competitive supremacy. What began as a slow accumulation of broadcasting revenue has become a wholesale transfer of authority, with the Board of Control for Cricket in India commanding a position no single nation has held since England's imperial-era monopoly on the game.

The Financial Juggernaut

The numbers tell an unambiguous story. The BCCI generates over 80% of global cricket revenue, driven by the Indian Premier League's $6 billion-plus media rights deal signed with Star Sports and Viacom. The IPL's per-match media value of approximately $13.4 million now exceeds the English Premier League's $11 million and trails only the NFL's $35 million, despite its season lasting just eight weeks.

IPL franchise valuations have crossed the billion-dollar mark. When Sanjiv Goenka's RPSG Group paid $930 million for the Lucknow Super Giants, it signaled that cricket franchises could rival the values of major European football clubs. Global private equity firms including Blackstone, KKR, and Partners Group are now pursuing IPL stakes, according to Reuters.

"The IPL can certainly rival—and in some cases outperform—U.S. leagues on investor returns, even if the absolute scale differs."

— Mohit Burman, co-owner, Punjab Kings

On the Field: A Tighter Race Than Expected

India's commercial dominance has been matched by sustained competitive excellence. The team won the T20 World Cup, Champions Trophy, and Asia Cup since 2024, prompting England's Phil Salt to concede that India had replaced his country as "the trendsetters in the global game."

Yet the latest ICC rankings delivered a reminder that financial supremacy does not guarantee perpetual on-field dominance. Australia dethroned India from the No. 1 Test ranking in May—the first time India has lost that position since October 2016. Australia lead with 116 rating points, followed by New Zealand at 115 and India at 114, the second-tightest margin since Test rankings began in 2003.

On the Test Championship points table, however, India remain firmly at the top with 360 points, 64 clear of second-placed Australia.

The Global Imbalance

India's ascendancy has created what critics describe as a "metropolis and its struggling provinces" dynamic. Indian broadcasters dictate global calendars, Indian sponsors shape tournament structures, and BCCI interests increasingly determine scheduling priorities. Smaller cricket nations, particularly in the Caribbean, Sri Lanka, and South Africa, struggle to secure fixtures against top teams, eroding the competitive ecosystem.

Even England's cricketing body operates with a fraction of the BCCI's resources, a stark reversal from the era when the English board refused to grant two extra tickets to Indian officials at the 1983 World Cup final—a snub that catalyzed India's push to host the 1987 tournament and ultimately seize control of the sport's economics.

What's Next

The next frontier is ownership-driven globalization. Indian investors now control franchises in South Africa's CSA T20 League, the Caribbean Premier League, and other domestic tournaments. Whether this expansion strengthens global cricket or further concentrates power in Indian hands will define the sport's trajectory for the next decade.
